I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Michael, a 26-year-old European American fisherman, has been grappling with intense psychological distress since his experiences of torture several months ago. Married and deeply committed to his family life, Michael's world has dramatically changed due to the lingering effects of that traumatic event. The trauma left deep emotional scars that Michael carries with him every day. He has become hypersensitive to certain triggers, particularly those involving auditory stimuli like hearing babies cry or riding on public transport, such as a bus. These triggers often send him into a state of high alert and intense distress. For example, he recalls an instance where his daughter's cries during a family outing triggered a sudden wave of rage and panic within him. This reaction is not just emotional but also physiological; when these triggers activate, Michael feels his body reenact the positions it was in during the torture, accompanied by physical pain in the same areas. One day, after hearing a baby cry on a bus, he experienced an intense flashback, reliving moments of his trauma. The vivid memories and accompanying rage were overwhelming, leaving him feeling physically exhausted and emotionally drained. This memory recall triggered a cascade of threats and vulnerabilities that made it difficult for Michael to feel safe in any environment where such triggers might arise again. The constant threat perception has significantly impacted his daily life. He feels unsafe unless he is positioned with his back against a wall, ensuring he can see everything happening around him. His heightened vigilance extends to intrusively listening for sounds that could indicate someone entering his home and noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment. This hyper-vigilant state has made it challenging for Michael to relax even in familiar settings. For instance, on one fishing trip, the sound of a boat engine reminded him of the noise he heard during the torture, triggering another memory and sending him into a panic attack. In this moment, his body reenacted the painful positions from the trauma, intensifying his sense of vulnerability and threat. The recurrence of such experiences has made Michael increasingly avoid situations that might trigger these memories and subsequent threats. His marriage has also been affected by these changes. His wife notices how he avoids certain activities and places because they activate his triggers. She worries about his constant state of alertness, as it affects their quality time together and her own sense of safety around him. Michael's fear of being vulnerable has grown significantly since the trauma. He often feels on edge, believing that any moment could bring a reminder of his past experiences. This constant threat monitoring reinforces his memories, making them feel more vivid and distressing over time. The cycle becomes self-reinforcing: his triggers activate memories, which in turn heighten his sense of threat, leading to further avoidance behaviors. What finally brought Michael to seek help was the realization that these symptoms were not only impacting him but also affecting those closest to him. He is most afraid of losing control and hurting someone he loves due to an uncontrollable rage or panic attack triggered by unexpected memories. At the same time, he hopes for a return to normalcy where he can feel safe and connected with his family without constant fear and distress. Michael's current state is marked by intense anxiety and hypervigilance, compounded by vivid and painful memories that are triggered by everyday sounds and situations. He is deeply motivated to regain control over his life and find ways to mitigate the overwhelming emotional and physical responses to these triggers.
